docs.title: Home
docs.text:
FielDHub

Design of experiments for life sciences

An R package and Shiny app that randomizes field, greenhouse and laboratory experiments, with a field map and a field book for every design.

Get started Browse the designs

FielDHub is a free, open-source R package and Shiny app for the design of experiments. It randomizes field, greenhouse and laboratory experiments: completely randomized (CRD), randomized complete block (RCBD), Latin square, factorial, split-plot, split-split-plot and strip-plot designs; square, rectangular and alpha lattices, incomplete block and row-column designs; and the unreplicated, augmented, partially replicated (p-rep) and sparse designs used in plant breeding and multi-location trials. It serves agriculture, plant breeding, forestry, and animal and biological sciences.

Every design comes with a field map and a field book. Every design in the app is also an R function with the same arguments, so a script can reproduce what the app made.

docs.title: What’s new in 1.7.5
docs.text:
• Design-aware trait simulation. stats::simulate(x) generates trait data for all 21 field designs using their treatment and experimental units.
  • Optional spatial correlation. Simulate field variation on physical row and column coordinates. The Shiny app uses the same simulator for tables, heatmaps, and downloads.

docs.title: What’s new in 1.7.0
docs.text:
• A new design. augmented_row_column() builds augmented row-column designs, in which every check appears once in every row or every column of the field. It has its own page in the app under Unreplicated Designs.
  • One style for every field map. One muted colour per replication or block, white alleys between them, grey lines around incomplete blocks, a white grid around every plot, and one muted colour per check.
  • Better partially replicated designs. An optional rule keeps the copies of an entry in distinct rows and columns (rowcol_penalty), and the spreading optimizer is much faster.
  • A refreshed app. New Welcome, Help and About pages: the Welcome page links to every design, and Help gives each design its guide, reference page and offline help() command.

See the release notes for every change, including the changes to results for a given seed.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
From CRAN:

install.packages("FielDHub")

The development version, from GitHub:

remotes::install_github("DidierMurilloF/FielDHub")

docs.title: Launch the app
docs.text:
library(FielDHub)
run_app()

The app’s dependencies install with the package, and it needs Shiny 1.8.1 or newer. To keep other sessions responsive while a long design runs, install mirai and start the app with run_app(workers = 2L). Workers need an installed FielDHub; without mirai, or when running from the package source, designs run in the app’s own session.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• A field map of every location, ready for reports.
  • A field book with plot numbers, rows, columns and entries, to download and load into a database or field app.
  • Simulated data. The app can simulate a response variable along with the randomization, for teaching and for testing an analysis before the season.
  • A reproducible record. write_design() saves a design or a standalone replay script, read_design() reads it back, and reproduce_design() rebuilds it from its recorded inputs and seed.

docs.title: Example: a multiple diagonal arrangement
docs.text:
A project needs to test 280 genotypes in a field of 16 rows and 20 columns, split among three experiments. Four checks are placed on diagonals across the experiments and fill 40 plots, 12.5% of the field. To get the same design in the app and in a script, use the same seed, here 1249.

diagonal <- diagonal_arrangement(
  nrows = 16,
  ncols = 20,
  lines = 280,
  checks = 4,
  plotNumber = 101,
  splitBy = "row",
  seed = 1249,
  kindExpt = "DBUDC",
  blocks = c(100, 100, 80),
  exptName = c("Expt1", "Expt2", "Expt3")
)

docs.title: Example: a partially replicated design
docs.text:
Partially replicated (p-rep) designs are common in early-generation trials: some entries are replicated and the rest appear once. Here 75 entries appear twice and 138 entries once, in a field of 16 rows and 18 columns (288 plots), with seed 77.

pREP <- partially_replicated(
  nrows = 16,
  ncols = 18,
  repGens = c(138, 75),
  repUnits = c(1, 2),
  planter = "serpentine",
  plotNumber = 1,
  exptName = "ExptA",
  locationNames = "FARGO",
  seed = 77
)

docs.title: For teaching
docs.text: FielDHub is used in courses on statistics, experimental design and plant breeding. Students see the randomization, the field layout and the data in one place; simulated responses give them a data set to analyse from the first class; and because every design is an R function with a seed, an assignment can give each student the same randomization, or a different one.

docs.title: Documentation and help
docs.text:
• The FielDHub website has a guide for every design, worked examples and the function reference.
  • In R, help("diagonal_arrangement", package = "FielDHub") and the other help pages work offline.
  • Video tutorials walk through the app.
  • Found a bug or missing a design? Open an issue.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text: If you use FielDHub, please cite the paper in the Journal of Open Source Software. Run citation("FielDHub") in R for the reference.

docs.text:
Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful.

docs.text:

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.

docs.title: Enforcement Guidelines
docs.text: Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

docs.title: 1. Correction
docs.text:
Community Impact: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

Consequence: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

docs.title: 2. Warning
docs.text:
Community Impact: A violation through a single incident or series of actions.

Consequence: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

docs.title: 3. Temporary Ban
docs.text:
Community Impact: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior.

Consequence: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

Community Impact: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

Consequence: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

docs.title: Contributing to FielDHub
docs.text:
First of all, thanks for considering contributing to FielDHub! 👍 It's people like you that make it rewarding for us - the project maintainers - to work on FielDHub. 😊

FielDHub is an open-source project, maintained by people who care.

docs.title: Code of conduct
docs.text: Please note that this project is released with a Contributor Code of Conduct. By participating in this project you agree to abide by its terms.

docs.title: How you can contribute
docs.text: There are several ways you can contribute to this project. If you want to know more about why and how to contribute to open source projects like this one, see this Open Source Guide.

docs.title: Share the love ❤️
docs.text:
Think FielDHub is useful? Let others discover it, by telling them in person, via Twitter or a blog post.

Using FielDHub for a paper you are writing? Consider citing it.

docs.title: Ask a question ⁉️
docs.text:
Using FielDHub and got stuck? Browse the documentation to see if you can find a solution. Still stuck? Post your question as an issue on GitHub. While we cannot offer user support, we'll try to do our best to address it, as questions often lead to better documentation or the discovery of bugs.

Want to ask a question in private? Contact the package maintainer by email.

docs.title: Propose an idea 💡
docs.text:
Have an idea for a new FielDHub feature? Take a look at the documentation and issue list to see if it isn't included or suggested yet. If not, suggest your idea as an issue on GitHub. While we can't promise to implement your idea, it helps to:

  • Explain in detail how it would work.
  • Keep the scope as narrow as possible.

See below if you want to contribute code for your idea as well.

docs.title: Report a bug 🐛
docs.text:
Using FielDHub and discovered a bug? That's annoying! Don't let others have the same experience and report it as an issue on GitHub so we can fix it. A good bug report makes it easier for us to do so, so please include:

  • Your operating system name and version (e.g. Mac OS 10.13.6).
  • Any details about your local setup that might be helpful in troubleshooting.
  • Detailed steps to reproduce the bug.

docs.title: Improve the documentation 📖
docs.text: Noticed a typo on the website? Think a function could use a better example? Good documentation makes all the difference, so your help to improve it is very welcome!

docs.title: The website
docs.text: This website is generated with Material for MkDocs from the documentation in the code, the vignettes and the Markdown files of the repository; see Preview the MkDocs website. You can propose a file change to improve documentation, or report an issue and we can point you in the right direction.

docs.title: Function documentation
docs.text:
Functions are described as comments near their code and translated to documentation using roxygen2. If you want to improve a function description:

  1. Go to R/ directory in the code repository.
  2. Look for the file that holds the function: an exported function f() is in R/fct_f.R (see Source layout for the other files).
  3. Propose a file change to update the function documentation in the roxygen comments (starting with #').

docs.title: Contribute code 📝
docs.text: Care to fix bugs or implement new functionality for FielDHub? Awesome! 👏 Have a look at the issue list and leave a comment on the things you want to work on. See also the development guidelines below.

docs.title: Development guidelines
docs.text:
From the repository root, run source("dev/run_dev.R") to load the source package and start the app. This path does not need a configuration file, detach packages, clear your workspace, or regenerate documentation. Stop the app normally before reloading changed source. Installed-package users run FielDHub::run_app(). The standard app dependencies are installed with the package. The root app.R returns the app object for source-based Shiny deployment.

Regenerate documentation separately with devtools::document() when changing roxygen comments.

FielDHub contains compiled C++ code (cpp11) for its block engine. Building from source, including source("dev/run_dev.R") and the root app.R, which call pkgload::load_all(), needs a C++17 toolchain (Rtools on Windows, the Xcode command line tools on macOS) and a writable package directory, because load_all() compiles into src/. Docker images install the package at build time and need neither at run time. After editing src/, run cpp11::cpp_register(). The engine is clean-room code: do not read or copy the source of GPL packages such as blocksdesign; see inst/PROVENANCE.md. Rscript --vanilla tools/check-launchers.R . checks both entry-script contracts without starting a server or changing the R session.

We try to follow the GitHub flow for development.

  1. Fork this repo and clone it to your computer. To learn more about this process, see this guide.
  2. If you have forked and cloned the project before and it has been a while since you worked on it, pull changes from the original repo to your clone by using git pull upstream master.
  3. Open the RStudio project file (.Rproj).
  4. Make your changes:
    • Add a plain-R regression test that fails before fixing a defect, then implement the fix. Keep scientific logic out of Shiny modules. Test app behaviour through the plain functions a page calls, or with shiny::testServer() for a module's reactive contract; do not add browser tests (shinytest2, screenshots).
    • Run the full tests with NOT_CRAN=true. Tests check properties of the output (counts, coordinates, efficiencies against independent references), not recorded copies of it. Announce deliberate scientific output changes and the affected inputs in NEWS.
    • For output-preserving refactors, compare complete fixed-seed results with the previous implementation using identical(). Preserve supplied labels, field-book column types, RNG state, and process options.
    • Document your code (see function documentation above).
    • Run R CMD check --as-cran, build the UI without starting a session, and inspect the completed check log. A development-version NOTE is expected; other findings require investigation. Check correctness lint and core coverage locally with Rscript inst/ci/lint-changed-lines.R <base-sha> <head-sha> and Rscript inst/ci/compare-core-coverage.R <base-dir> <head-dir>.
  5. Commit and push your changes.
  6. Submit a pull request.

Design pages must never be blank while a requested operation is running. Run and Randomize need a centered spinner and short status inside each result tab's content area, including queued background jobs. The loading state replaces that tab's content until it is ready; do not add a banner above or outside the tabs. Tab switching must keep the feedback visible in the selected tab without forced scrolling. Plots and tables also need output-loading indicators. Clear task feedback on success, validation failure, worker failure and disconnection; show an explanation for errors. Do not rely only on output-recalculation spinners for asynchronous work, or display a percentage unless the operation reports real progress. Verify these states in a real browser; keep automated tests at the plain-helper and UI-contract level.

Maintainers follow the release checklist, including the full R and platform matrix, reconstruction checks, deployment validation, and reviewed performance benchmarks. Use a minor release for deliberate API or behavior changes; keep migration guidance alongside the change. The deployment guide documents the locked Docker build and distinguishes source checks from verified image execution.

Scientific changes also need independent count, geometry, or numerical checks. Use the plain helpers in tests/testthat/helper-invariants.R, specify expected levels from the inputs (including missing groups), and include corrupted fixtures to prove the checks detect failures. See the scientific validation guide for the family-by-family checks, reference calculations, and computational limits.

docs.title: Source layout
docs.text:
Read the architecture and compatibility guide and the step-by-step design/format extension guide before adding a new engine or format. The Latin rectangle is a complete registry-driven example, including the shared app page and independent tests.

The .mailmap normalizes display-name aliases using an already shared email address. Propose other identity mappings with the contributor's confirmation; do not guess from similar names or rewrite historical commits. The release owner and independent reviewer are agreed by maintainers for each release.

Each file in R/ is named <prefix>_<topic>.R. The prefix says what the file is responsible for; the topic says what it holds (for example engine_diagonal_checks.R, layout_planting_path.R, result_methods.R).

Prefix Responsibility fct_ exported design engines (one per exported function) engine_ internal randomization/allocation/optimization helpers layout_ field coordinates, planting paths, layout options render_ drawing only (desplot/ggplot/heatmap data) io_ uploads, exports, archives validate_ input validators and parsers result_ result constructor, schema, S3 methods, reproduction sim_ response simulation api_ cross-cutting public documentation app_, mod_ Shiny layer only
  • A fct_ file is named after its exported function (fct_RCBD.R holds RCBD()). Helpers used only by that function may sit beside it.
  • Exception: the allocation and pair-swap result builders (new_fieldhub_allocation(), validate_fieldhub_allocation(), new_fieldhub_optimization(), validate_fieldhub_optimization()) live in fct_do_optim.R and fct_swap_pairs.R, not in result_ files. Each validator reads the arguments of its engine (formals(do_optim), formals(swap_pairs)), so a result_ file would depend on the fct_ file that depends on it. fct_reproduce_design.R calls both validators.
  • api_ files hold roxygen documentation only: api_vocabulary.R (argument names) and api_result_contract.R (the structure of every result, shared by all designs, so it is api_ rather than result_).
  • app_/mod_ files hold the Shiny wiring. Plain helpers the app uses (reading an input, preparing a simulation or an export) live in core prefixes, where they are unit-tested and count toward core coverage. Core files (every other prefix) never refer to app_/mod_ code and make no shiny, DT, bslib or shinyjs calls.
  • Dependencies between files go one way: no file may depend, directly or through other files, on a file that depends on it. When two files call each other, move the mutually dependent functions into one file, or into a lower layer that both use.
  • R loads these files in alphabetical order, so top-level code (such as x <- f()) may only use objects defined above it in the same file.

Three files are exceptions:

  • cpp11.R is generated by cpp11::cpp_register(); never edit it by hand.
  • globals.R declares the column names used in non-standard evaluation.
  • run_app.R holds run_app(), the exported launcher of the Shiny app.

Tests live in tests/testthat/test_<feature>.R, one table-driven file per feature, and check user-facing contracts only. They are plain R: app logic is tested through plain functions or shiny::testServer(), never through a browser. test_package_hygiene.R checks the source layout (prefixes, one fct_ file per exported function, no core reference to the Shiny layer, no dependency cycle between core files). Structural checks that must also run under R CMD check, where R/ is not installed, inspect the namespace with core_functions() and app_functions() from helper-source.R. The core coverage check (inst/ci/compare-core-coverage.R) measures every R/ file except app_*, mod_* and run_app.R.

docs.title: Preview the MkDocs website
docs.text:
Install R, Pandoc, Python, a C++17 toolchain, and the package dependencies from DESCRIPTION, plus the documentation packages pkgdown, xml2, and yaml. The build installs this checkout into a temporary library before rendering.

python3 -m venv /tmp/fieldhub-docs-venv
source /tmp/fieldhub-docs-venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
FIELDHUB_DOCS_PYTHON="$(command -v python)" Rscript tools/build-site.R
mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/FielDHub/. R generates the Markdown and figures in .mkdocs-src/, and MkDocs writes the built site to .mkdocs-site/. Rerun the R script after editing a vignette, an Rd topic, or index.Rmd. The build renders the home page, all vignettes and Rd topics. The historical /dev/ tree mirrors the published documentation so existing development links continue to resolve. Both trees use production canonical URLs. Legacy reference/fieldLayout.html redirects to field_layout.html, and reference/pipe.html redirects to the reference index.

docs.title: Releasing FielDHub
docs.text: Release decisions, repository settings, publishing, and tags belong to the maintainers. A clean local check is not evidence that remote CI has passed.

docs.title: Prepare the candidate
docs.text:
1. Choose the release scope and version. Scientific output changes, classed errors, deprecations, or changed defaults must be explicit in NEWS. Do not release the modernization's behavior changes as an undocumented patch.
  2. Review DESCRIPTION, both NEWS files, generated documentation, and the migration examples. Keep a development version between releases.
  3. Give a second reviewer the scientific changes, old/new comparisons, deliberate snapshot changes, and any remaining limitations. Agree on a release owner and a backup reviewer; do not infer approval from green CI.
  4. Complete a licensing review with the appropriate copyright holders. Earlier releases contained efficiency helpers marked as sourced from the GPL-licensed blocksdesign package while FielDHub declared MIT. Replacing those helpers and removing the dependency do not themselves resolve obligations for historical distributions. Record the maintainer's resolution before publishing; do not infer that an unchanged package license is sufficient.

docs.title: Required evidence
docs.text:
• Run the complete plain-R tests, including the tests skipped on CRAN:
NOT_CRAN=true Rscript -e 'devtools::test(stop_on_failure=TRUE)'
Rscript -e 'pkgload::load_all(); invisible(FielDHub:::app_ui(NULL))'
Rscript -e 'rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck(args=c("--no-manual", "--as-cran"), error_on="warning")'
  • Read the completed 00check.log, including * DONE. Development builds may have the large-version-components NOTE; remove that cause for a release. Investigate every other NOTE, warning, or error. Network-unavailable checks must be rerun with network access before submission.
  • Confirm the remote check matrix passes on macOS, Linux, Windows, R-devel, oldrel, and the declared minimum R version. The three current-R platforms run on every PR and push. Manually dispatch R-CMD-check-extended against the exact candidate revision before publishing; its Linux R-devel, oldrel and minimum-R checks also run weekly and on v* tags. Keep the required check names macos-latest (release) and ubuntu-latest (release) stable.
  • Confirm pkgdown, changed-line correctness lint, and the core coverage gate pass. Review legacy-object compatibility and design/simulation reconstruction tests. No Shiny server or browser tests are required: exercise business logic as plain R functions and construct the UI without starting a session.
  • Build the deployment image and verify its non-root runtime and locked dependencies. A package check does not validate deployment.

docs.title: Record performance and quality
docs.text:
Install the exact candidate into a separate library. From the repository root, run the scripts against it, choosing output files that do not already exist:

Rscript tools/check-release-tools.R .
Rscript tools/benchmark-dimensions.R dimensions.csv /path/to/candidate-library
Rscript tools/benchmark-spatial.R spatial.csv /path/to/candidate-library
Rscript tools/benchmark-exports.R exports.csv /path/to/candidate-library
Rscript tools/benchmark-optimizers.R optimizers.csv /path/to/candidate-library

For a complete, comparable record use tools/run-benchmarks.R instead. Install each exact revision into a separate library first; the revision argument labels that installation, it does not fetch or install code. Run both sequentially on the same idle host with identical dependency versions:

Rscript tools/run-benchmarks.R baseline-results /path/to/baseline-library FULL_BASELINE_SHA
Rscript tools/run-benchmarks.R candidate-results /path/to/candidate-library FULL_CANDIDATE_SHA
Rscript tools/compare-benchmarks.R baseline-results candidate-results comparison.csv

The comparison rejects mismatched environments, measurement-script hashes, workloads, missing cases and duplicate cases. Runtime increases over both 25% and 10 ms, allocation increases over 25%, unavailable allocation profiling, reduced optimizer minimum distance, and changed stop diagnostics require review. These are review thresholds, not scientific tolerances or promises about performance. Re-run noisy measurements. An optional fourth argument supplies a CSV of reviewed exceptions containing case, metric, baseline, candidate, baseline_revision, candidate_revision, and a substantive reason. Copy the exact values from the report; stale, duplicate or unnecessary exceptions fail. Keep the original report, new report, and explanations with the release evidence.

The full suite requires the bounded factor search, separable simulator, indexed exporter and optimizer diagnostics. f06aaf01626bf390f985861c62c386656604b4d3 is the first frozen modernization baseline for this protocol, not a released version. The old 1.5.0 implementation cannot safely run the large cases (its factor subsets are exponential and spatial covariance is dense). Do not label an unsupported old-release comparison as passing or run it at those sizes. Use an independently bounded common-workload study for historical comparisons.

The manually dispatchable release-benchmarks workflow runs the same four benchmarks and retains CSV files and session information for 90 days. Copy the reviewed results into the permanent release assets before they expire. It accepts an optional full baseline SHA to run and compare on the same runner; without one, it collects candidate evidence but does not claim a regression gate passed. Remote workflow execution still requires a pushed branch.

Compare with the previous release on the same hardware, R version, and package versions, with no competing workloads. Record and explain regressions before publishing; repeat noisy measurements. Do not treat shared-runner timings as precise cross-release comparisons. Review optimizer quality and stop reasons, not just speed. largest_R_allocation_bytes measures the largest R allocation, not peak memory, and is NA when profiling is unavailable. Zero means profiling ran but recorded no numeric allocation event (small allocations can use R's existing allocation pools); it does not mean zero RAM.

docs.title: Publish and follow up
docs.text:
1. The maintainer checks required branch protection and approves the merge.
  2. Tag the exact reviewed release commit and publish the source and benchmark evidence. Verify historical tags against the corresponding CRAN sources.
  3. Submit to CRAN and resolve incoming checks; do not equate submission with acceptance. Announce affected inputs for any corrected scientific outputs.
  4. Publish the documentation, verify package installation and downloadable archives, and open the next development version.

Use opt-in issue reports for feedback. Do not add usage tracking or collect field books, treatment labels, or other experiment data without consent.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: FielDHub is an R package with a Shiny app. You can build a design in the app, or call the same design function from a script: both give the same field map and field book for the same inputs and seed.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
From CRAN:

install.packages("FielDHub")

The development version, from GitHub:

remotes::install_github("DidierMurilloF/FielDHub")

docs.title: Open the app
docs.text:
library(FielDHub)
run_app()

Choose a design from the menus, fill in its inputs and click Run!. The app shows the field map and the field book, and lets you download them.

docs.title: Make a design in R
docs.text:
Every design in the app is also a function. This one places 270 unreplicated entries and 4 checks in a field of 15 rows and 20 columns, with the checks on diagonals:

design <- diagonal_arrangement(
  nrows = 15, ncols = 20, lines = 270, checks = 4, seed = 1987
)

Every design is used in the same way:

print(design)           # a summary of the design
plot(design)            # the field map
head(design$fieldBook)  # the field book, one row per plot

The seed makes the randomization reproducible: the same call gives the same design.

docs.title: Save and reproduce a design
docs.text:
write_design(design, "design.rds")

saved <- read_design("design.rds")
again <- reproduce_design(saved)

write_design() saves the design with its inputs and seed, read_design() reads it back, and reproduce_design() builds it again from that record.

docs.title: Articles
docs.text: Each design has a guide that builds it twice: in the Shiny app and with its R function.

docs.title: Unreplicated Designs
docs.text:
• Single Diagonal Arrangement

    Unreplicated entries with checks on diagonals, in one field or split among several experiments.

    diagonal_arrangement()

  • Optimized Arrangement

    Unreplicated entries with checks placed at random and spread across the field.

    optimized_arrangement()

  • Augmented RCBD

    The same checks in every block, with unreplicated entries distributed among the blocks.

    RCBD_augmented()

  • Augmented Row-Column

    Unreplicated entries with every check once in each row or each column of the field.

    augmented_row_column()

  • Sparse Allocation

    Each entry is tested at a subset of the locations, in an unreplicated design at each one.

    sparse_allocation()

docs.title: Partially Replicated Designs
docs.text:
• Single and Multi-Location p-rep

    Some entries are replicated and the rest appear once, at one or several locations.

    partially_replicated()

  • Optimized Multi-Location p-rep

    Optimizes how the copies of each entry are shared among locations, then builds a p-rep design at each one.

    multi_location_prep()

docs.title: Lattice Designs
docs.text:
• Square Lattice

    Resolvable incomplete blocks for k² treatments in blocks of size k.

    square_lattice()

  • Rectangular Lattice

    Resolvable incomplete blocks for k(k + 1) treatments in blocks of size k.

    rectangular_lattice()

  • Alpha Lattice: alpha(0,1)

    Resolvable incomplete blocks for a flexible number of treatments and block sizes.

    alpha_lattice()

docs.title: Other Designs
docs.text:
• Completely Randomized Design (CRD)

    Treatments assigned to plots completely at random.

    CRD()

  • Randomized Complete Block Designs (RCBD)

    Every treatment once in each complete block, at one or several locations.

    RCBD()

  • Latin Square Design (LSD)

    Every treatment once in each row and each column of a square.

    latin_square()

  • Latin Rectangle Design

    Randomized cyclic Latin rectangle.

    latin_rectangle()

  • Factorial Designs

    All combinations of the levels of two or more factors, as a CRD or an RCBD.

    full_factorial()

  • Split-Plot Design

    Two factors, one on whole plots and one on sub-plots.

    split_plot()

  • Split-Split-Plot Design

    Three factors, on whole plots, sub-plots and sub-sub-plots.

    split_split_plot()

  • Strip-Plot Design

    Two factors applied in horizontal and vertical strips that cross in each block.

    strip_plot()

  • Incomplete Blocks Design (IBD)

    Resolvable incomplete blocks for a chosen number of treatments, replicates and block size.

    incomplete_blocks()

  • Resolvable Row-Column Design (RRCD)

    Resolvable designs that block in two directions, by rows and by columns.

    row_column()

docs.title: Augmented Randomized Complete Block Design
docs.text: This vignette shows how to generate an augmented randomized complete block design using both the FielDHub Shiny App and the scripting function RCBD_augmented() from the FielDHub package.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The augmented randomized complete block design is another option to overcome the problem of limited facilities or lack of seed when researchers want to test many treatments. In this kind of design, the approach is to build augmented blocks and allocate the same amount of controls in every block along with the treatments.

FielDHub includes a function to run such experimental designs, features include options to set the number of entries and the number of checks and augmented blocks for the experiment. Users can also choose to run the same experiment over multiple locations.

docs.title: Use case
docs.text: For example, we say a project needs to test 120 genotypes of cassava over two locations. In addition, the research includes four checks and six augmented blocks to carry out this experiment. This design setup comes out with 6 blocks of size 24 plots for a total of 144 plots that will be distributed in a field of 12 rows and 12 columns.

docs.title: Running the Shiny App
docs.text:
To launch the app you need to run either

FielDHub::run_app()

or

library(FielDHub)
run_app()

docs.title: 1. Using the FielDHub Shiny App
docs.text:
Once the app is running, go to Unreplicated Designs > RCBD Augmented

Then, follow the following steps where we will show how to generate an RCBD Augmented.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
1. Import entries’ list? Choose whether to import a list with entry numbers and names for genotypes or treatments.

    • If the selection is No, that means the app is going to generate synthetic data for entries and names of the treatment/genotypes based on the user inputs.

    • If the selection is Yes, the entries list must fulfill a specific format and must be a .csv file. The file must have the columns ENTRY and NAME. The ENTRY column must have a unique entry integer number for each treatment/genotype. The column NAME must have a unique name that identifies each treatment/genotype. Both ENTRY and NAME must be unique, duplicates are not allowed. In the following table, we show an example of the entries list format. This example has an entry list with four checks and 8 treatments/genotypes. It is crucial to allocate the checks in the top part of the file.

ENTRY NAME 1 CHECK1 2 CHECK2 3 CHECK3 4 G-4 5 G-5 6 G-6 7 G-7 8 G-8 9 G-9 10 G-10 11 G-11 12 G-12

  1. Enter the number of stacked experiments in the Input # of Stacked Expts box. This means the number of times the experiment will be replicated. In our case we will perform just 1 experiment.

  2. On the augmented RCBD we have the option to choose whether we randomize the entries or not, with the Randomize Entries toggle button. It is recommended always randomized the treatments/entries but some researchers choose not to randomize treatments, this is often due to logistical issues.

  3. Enter the number of entries/treatments in the Input # of Entries box, which is 120 in our example experiment.

  4. Set the number of checks per block with the Checks per Block box. In our case, it is 5 checks.

  5. Set the number of blocks with Input # of Blocks box, which is 6 in our example.

The total number of plots in our field will be Input # of Stacked Expts(Input # of Entries + Input # of Blocks * Checks per Block), per location.

  1. Enter the number of locations in Input # of Locations. Set it as 2.

  2. Select serpentine or cartesian in the Plot Order Layout. For this example we will set the serpentine layout.

  3. To ensure that randomizations are consistent across sessions, we can set a random seed in the box labeled random seed. In this example, we will set it to 1987.

  4. Enter the starting plot number in the Starting Plot Number box. If the experiment has multiple locations, you must enter a comma separated list of numbers the length of the number of locations for the input to be valid.

To start a new plot-number range in each block, select Number plots by block and enter the Plot number increment between blocks (for example, 100). With a starting plot of 101, the blocks start at 101, 201, 301, and so on. The increment must be at least the number of plots per block. For stacked experiments, each additional rep receives a separate range: with five blocks and an increment of 100, the second rep starts at 601. Plot numbers do not overlap across reps within a location. Leave this option off for continuous numbering.

  1. Once we have entered the information for our experiment on the left side panel, click the Run! button to run the design.

  2. You will then be prompted to select the dimensions of the field from the list of options in the drop down in the middle of the screen with the box labeled Select dimensions of field. In our case, we will select 12 x 12.

  3. Click the Randomize! button to randomize the experiment with the set field dimensions and to see the output plots. If you change the dimensions again, you must re-randomize.

If you change any of the inputs on the left side panel after running an experiment initially, you have to click the Run and Randomize buttons again, to re-run with the new inputs.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: After you run the augmented RCBD in FielDHub and set the dimensions of the field, there are several ways to display the information contained in the field book. The first tab, Get Random, shows the option to change the dimensions of the field and re-randomize, as well as a reference guide for experiment design.

docs.title: Input Data
docs.text: On the second tab, Input Data, you can see all the entries in the randomization in a list, as well as a table of the checks with the number of times they appear in the field. In the list of entries, the reps for each check is included as well.

docs.title: Randomized Field
docs.text: The Randomized Field tab displays a graphical representation of the randomization of the entries in a field of the specified dimensions. The checks are all colored uniquely, showing the number of times they are distributed throughout the field. The display includes numbered labels for the rows and columns. You can copy the field as a table or save it directly as an Excel file with the Copy and Excel buttons at the top.

docs.title: Plot Number Field
docs.text: On the Plot Number Field tab, there is a table display of the field with the plots numbered according to the Plot Order Layout specified, either serpentine or cartesian. You can see the corresponding entries for each plot number in the field book. Like the Randomized Field tab, you can copy the table or save it as an Excel file with the Copy and Excel buttons.

docs.title: Field Book
docs.text: The Field Book displays all the information on the experimental design in a table format. It contains the specific plot number and the row and column address of each entry, as well as the corresponding treatment on that plot. This table is searchable, and we can filter the data in relevant columns.

docs.title: 2. Using the FielDHub function: RCBD_augmented()
docs.text:
You can run the same design with the function RCBD_augmented() in the FielDHub package.

First, you need to load the FielDHub package typing,

library(FielDHub)

Then, you can enter the information describing the above design like this:

aug_RCBD <- RCBD_augmented(
  lines = 120,
  checks = 4,
  b = 6, 
  repsExpt = 1, 
  l = 2,
  random = TRUE,
  exptName = "Cassava_2022", 
  plotNumber = c(1001, 2001),
  locationNames = c("FARGO", "CASSELTON"),
  nrows = 12,
  ncols = 12,
  seed = 1987
)

docs.title: Details on the inputs entered in RCBD_augmented() above
docs.text:
The description for the inputs that we used to generate the design,

  • lines = 120 is the number of entries
  • checks = 4 is the number of checks in each augmented block.
  • b = 6 is the number of augmented blocks.
  • repsExpt = 1 is the number of reps for the experiment.
  • l = 2 is the number of locations.
  • random = TRUE it means both treatment/entries and checks will be randomized.
  • exptName = "Cassava_2022" is an optional name for the experiment.
  • plotNumber = c(1001,2001) are the starting plot number for each location respectively, or a single number for 1 location.
  • locationNames = c("FARGO", "CASSELTON") are the values for representing respective name for each location.
  • nrows = 12 is the number of rows in the field. It is optional
  • ncols = 12 is the number of columns in the field. It is optional.
  • seed = 1987 is the random seed to replicate identical randomizations.

docs.title: Print aug_RCBD output
docs.text:
To print a summary of the information that is in the object aug_RCBD, we can use the generic function print().

print(aug_RCBD)

docs.title: Access to aug_RCBD output
docs.text:
The function RCBD_augmented() returns a list consisting of all the information displayed in the output tabs in the FielDHub app: design information, plot layout, plot numbering, entries list, and field book. These are accessible by the $ operator, i.e. aug_RCBD$layoutRandom or aug_RCBD$fieldBook.

aug_RCBD$fieldBook is a list containing information about every plot in the field, with information about the location of the plot and the treatment in each plot. As seen in the output below, the field book has columns for ID, EXPT, LOCATION, YEAR, PLOT, ROW, COLUMN, CHECKS, ENTRY, and TREATMENT.

Let us see the first 10 rows of the field book for this experiment.

field_book <- aug_RCBD$fieldBook
head(field_book, 10)

docs.title: Plot field layout
docs.text: For plotting the layout in function of the coordinates ROW and COLUMN in the field book object we can use the generic function plot() as follow,

docs.title: Plot layout for location 1
docs.text:
plot(aug_RCBD)

It is possible to pass more arguments to plot() such as the specific location. For example, you can plot the layout for location 2.

docs.title: Plot layout for location 2
docs.text: plot(aug_RCBD, l = 2)

docs.title: Plot numbering by block and rep
docs.text:
The same option is available from R through plotIncrement. A start per location automatically reserves b * plotIncrement numbers per rep. To choose rep starts explicitly for one location, pass a vector such as plotNumber = c(101, 1001); overlapping ranges are rejected. Filler plots keep number zero, and the entry randomization and field positions are unchanged.

numbered <- RCBD_augmented(lines = 50, checks = 3, b = 5, repsExpt = 2,
                           plotNumber = 101, plotIncrement = 100, seed = 23)
aggregate(PLOT ~ EXPT + BLOCK, data = numbered$fieldBook, FUN = min)

docs.title: Alpha Lattice Design
docs.text: This vignette shows how to generate an alpha lattice design using both the FielDHub Shiny App and the scripting function alpha_lattice() from the FielDHub package.

docs.title: 1. Using the FielDHub Shiny App
docs.text:
To launch the app you need to run either

FielDHub::run_app()

or

library(FielDHub)
run_app()

Once the app is running, go to Lattice Designs > Alpha Lattice

Then, follow the following steps where we will show how to generate this kind of design with 55 treatments and 3 reps.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
1. Import entries’ list? Choose whether to import a list with entry numbers and names for genotypes or treatments.

    • If the selection is No, that means the app is going to generate synthetic data for entries and names of the treatment/genotypes based on the user inputs.

    • If the selection is Yes, the entries list must fulfill a specific format and must be a .csv file. The file must have the columns ENTRY and NAME. The ENTRY column must have a unique entry integer number for each treatment. The column NAME must have a unique name that identifies each treatment. Both ENTRY and NAME must be unique, duplicates are not allowed. In the following table, we show an example of the entries list format. This example has an entry list with 12 treatments.

ENTRY NAME 1 GenotypeA 2 GenotypeB 3 GenotypeC 4 GenotypeD 5 GenotypeE 6 GenotypeF 7 GenotypeG 8 GenotypeH 9 GenotypeI 10 GenotypeJ 11 GenotypeK 12 GenotypeL

  1. Input the number of treatments in the Input # of Treatments box. In the alpha lattice design, the number of treatments must be a composite number. In this case, set it to 55.

  2. Select the number of replications of these treatments with the Input # of Full Reps box. Set it to 3.

  3. Set the number of plots in each incomplete block in the Input # of Plots per IBlock box. Set it to 5.

  4. Enter the number of locations in Input # of Locations. We will run this experiment over a single location, so set it to 1.

  5. Select serpentine or cartesian in the Plot Order Layout. For this example we will use the default cartesian layout.

  6. Enter the starting plot number in the Starting Plot Number box. If the experiment has multiple locations, you must enter a comma separated list of numbers the length of the number of locations for the input to be valid. Set it to 101.

  7. Enter a name for the location of the experiment in the Input Location box. If there are multiple locations, each name must be in a comma separated list. For this example, set it to "FARGO".

  8. To ensure that randomizations are consistent across sessions, we can set a random seed in the box labeled random seed. In this example, we will set it to 1235.

  9. Once we have entered the information for our experiment on the left side panel, click the Run! button to run the design.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: After you run an alpha lattice design in FielDHub, there are several ways to display the information contained in the field book.

docs.title: Field Layout
docs.text: When you first click the run button on an alpha lattice design, FielDHub displays the Field Layout tab, which shows the entries and their arrangement in the field. In the box below the display, you can change the layout of the field or change the location displayed. You can also display a heatmap over the field by changing Type of Plot to Heatmap. To view a heatmap, you must first simulate an experiment over the described field with the Simulate! button. A pop-up window will appear where you can choose the trait to simulate and enter its mean and plot-error (residual) standard deviation (SD). The simulated values include the treatment and design effects of the layout.

docs.title: Field Book
docs.text: The Field Book displays all the information on the experimental design in a table format. It contains the specific plot number and the row and column address of each entry, as well as the corresponding treatment on that plot. This table is searchable, and we can filter the data in relevant columns. If we have simulated data for a heatmap, an additional column for that variable appears in the Field Book.

docs.title: 2. Using the FielDHub function: alpha_lattice()
docs.text:
You can run the same design with a function in the FielDHub package, alpha_lattice().

First, you need to load the FielDHub package typing,

library(FielDHub)

Then, you can enter the information describing the above design like this:

alpha <- alpha_lattice(
  t = 55,
  reps = 3,
  k = 5, 
  l = 1,      
  plotNumber = 101, 
  locationNames = "FARGO", 
  seed = 1235
)

docs.title: Details on the inputs entered in alpha_lattice() above
docs.text:
The description for the inputs that we used to generate the design,

  • t = 55 is the number of treatments.
  • reps =3 is the number of replicates.
  • k = 5 is the number of plots per incomplete block.
  • l = 1 is the number of locations.
  • plotNumber = 101 is the starting plot number.
  • locationNames = "FARGO" is an optional name for each location.
  • seed = 1235 is the random seed to replicate identical randomizations.

docs.title: Layers and direction of dependencies
docs.text:
Layer Responsibilities Must not do Public engines (fct_, engine_, validate_) Validate inputs, randomize, optimize, construct results Depend on Shiny, display dialogs, install packages, change caller options Results (result_) Schema, declarative engine registry, replay, S3 presentation Evaluate function names or handlers supplied by saved metadata Layout/render/simulation (layout_, render_, sim_) Coordinates, drawing, numerical simulation Re-randomize a saved design merely to display it I/O (io_) Parse uploads, validated format dispatch, plain CSV exports Treat a CSV field book as a complete replay record App (app_) Declarative page controls, argument builders, one generic module Duplicate engine logic or mutate the accepted result when controls change

The standard app dependencies are in Imports. run_app() checks its runtime packages and reports an installation command if needed; it does not install anything. source("dev/run_dev.R") is the source-development launcher, while deployed images start the installed package. Both use native Shiny without a framework configuration file.

Every app request is converted to a plain named argument list and sent to a whitelisted public engine. A completed design is an immutable snapshot for layout, simulation and downloads. With opt-in workers > 0, installed-package jobs use a private mirai pool; source development remains synchronous. Workers close when the app stops. The 100 MiB process-wide Shiny upload setting is scoped to the app lifetime and restored afterward, not on each session disconnect.

docs.title: Results and randomness
docs.text:
A design has class c("fieldhub_<key>", "FielDHub"), infoDesign, fieldBook and schema-1 metadata. The common book keys are ID, LOCATION, and PLOT; the registry declares additional columns for each design. Extra columns are allowed. Field coordinates belong to the layout contract; some engines record them at construction, while others offer multiple layouts. PLOT alone is not a universal unique key for split units, fillers or multiple locations.

Metadata records the design key, schema version, effective seed, RNG kinds, package version and effective parameters. An explicit seed restores the caller stream; an omitted seed consumes exactly one automatically selected seed, then isolates all internal randomization. Failed input validation should occur before that draw. Numerical optimizers can also depend on R, dependencies and platform; metadata is not a guarantee of cross-version bit-identical reconstruction.

x <- latin_rectangle(5, rows = 3, seed = 27)
x$metadata[c("design", "schema_version", "seed", "package_version")]

#> $design
#> [1] "latin_rectangle"
#> 
#> $schema_version
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $seed
#> [1] 27
#> 
#> $package_version
#> [1] "1.7.5"

stopifnot(identical(reproduce_design(x), x))

Allocation plans and pair-swap results have separate validated classes but use the same metadata/replay boundary. Legacy 1.5.x results still have their documented printing and plotting path. Missing historical parameters cannot be recovered automatically and must not be invented.

docs.title: Extension boundaries
docs.text:
The reviewed fieldhub_design_registry() is the single declaration of engine names and field-book extensions. New fixed-coordinate designs can declare generic layout/render handlers and a title, avoiding new dispatcher branches. Existing specialized S3 methods preserve established layouts and output. Optimization strategies live in plain engine helpers and record their choices as data; visualizations use the layout/render S3 boundary. Neither should leak UI concerns into scientific computation.

These are contributor interfaces for package code, not a mutable global plugin registry. External packages should use the documented public engines, field_layout(), replay and I/O APIs rather than depend on internal function names. Adding runtime third-party handlers would need a separate compatibility and security proposal. See the Adding designs and formats vignette for the concrete extension procedure and the Latin rectangle example.

docs.title: Versioned interchange
docs.text:
design_formats()

#>   format extension               media_type format_version readable writable
#> 1    rds       rds application/octet-stream              1     TRUE     TRUE
#> 2      r         R               text/plain              1    FALSE     TRUE

file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
write_design(x, file)
stopifnot(identical(read_design(file), x))
unlink(file)

Format version 1 and result schema version 1 are independent contracts. RDS uses R serialization version 2 and preserves the exact result. The validated reader rejects unknown result schemas and engines and does not replay or execute code. Only deserialize files from trusted sources. An R script is a write-only replay artifact, never an importer; inspect it before explicitly sourcing it. Script export declines oversized uploads/nonportable parameters rather than emitting a misleading incomplete program. App layout and field-book downloads are plain CSV files; field books include displayed simulated traits. These table downloads do not include companion metadata or reconstruction files.

No existing file is overwritten by write_design() unless overwrite = TRUE. Serialization happens first in a temporary file; the final copy is not an atomic filesystem transaction. Preserve backups of important outputs.

docs.title: Compatibility and release ownership
docs.text:
Scientific outputs for a fixed seed are part of the compatibility contract. Correctness fixes may change them, but require a regression, an independent scientific check, an explained snapshot diff and a NEWS entry naming affected inputs. Do not silently update snapshots to make a refactor pass. New public options retain old defaults unless a deliberate change is documented.

Deprecated public arguments retain an alias and a classed warning through at least one published minor release before removal is proposed. A schema change requires a version increment and an explicit migration/rejection policy. Internal extension changes must update the contributor guide and contract tests in the same change; they are not an undocumented third-party API promise.

Maintainers choose a release owner and an independent backup/reviewer for each release. Green checks do not confer scientific or publication approval. The repository’s RELEASING.md requires reviewed benchmarks, a platform/R matrix, deployment evidence, licensing resolution, NEWS and an exact release tag. Local verification does not establish remote CI or CRAN acceptance.

Feedback is opt-in through issues or the published maintainer contact. Request minimal synthetic reproductions; do not collect private field books or add telemetry. Review/release roles and contributor identities require agreement, not inference from activity counts or email similarity.

docs.title: Augmented Row-Column Design
docs.text: This vignette shows how to generate an augmented row-column design using both the FielDHub Shiny App and the scripting function augmented_row_column() from the FielDHub package.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
In early-generation trials there is usually seed for only one plot of each test entry. Augmented designs replicate a small number of checks across the field so that field trends and the residual variance can be estimated and the unreplicated tests can be compared.

An augmented row-column design controls field variation in two directions, rows and columns, in one complete rectangular field. In FielDHub’s version every check appears exactly once in every field line along one direction (every column, or every row), and every test entry appears exactly once.

FielDHub already offers two check-based designs. RCBD_augmented() blocks in one direction, and diagonal_arrangement() places checks in a systematic diagonal pattern. augmented_row_column() places the checks so that both row and column effects are estimable and then searches the check positions under a chosen statistical criterion.

Features include the field dimensions, the number of checks (or the check labels), test labels or an uploaded entry list, the check direction, one of three search criteria, multiple locations, serpentine or cartesian plot numbering, and reproducible results from a recorded seed.

docs.title: Attribution
docs.text:
The construction is that of Piepho and Williams (2026): an augmented row-column design generated from a small auxiliary array called a contraction. They show that the efficiency of the contraction and of the augmented design are closely linked, so a design can be described and searched through the small contraction rather than the whole field.

The square-array foundation is Bailey and Haines (2025): square fields (\(v = s\)) represented through a \(k \times t\) auxiliary block design, with results on connectedness and randomization. Square fields in FielDHub include these square-array designs.

FielDHub’s own contribution is the search for the check positions, the restricted placement rules adopted here, the orientation handling, the field book and the app. The search described below is FielDHub’s own method. It is not part of the published construction, and the published articles are not responsible for it.

All computation is FielDHub code. No published design is copied into the package; published layouts are cited only as literature.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
The method works in a mathematical orientation with \(v\) rows and \(s\) columns, in which each check appears once in every mathematical column. The section on the check direction explains how this maps to physical field rows and columns.

Symbol Meaning \(v\) Plots in each line along the check direction (mathematical rows) \(s\) Lines along the check direction (mathematical columns) \(k\) Number of checks, \(2 \le k < v\) \(n = vs\) Number of plots \(T = (v - k)s\) Number of test entries, each on one plot \(v^* = T + k\) Number of treatments (tests plus checks) \(u\) Replications: 1 for each test, \(s\) for each check \(r_h\) Number of check plots in mathematical row \(h\)

Every check occupies \(s\) plots, so the checks take \(ks\) plots and the tests the remaining \((v-k)s\).

docs.title: The contraction
docs.text:
The check positions are described by a \(k \times s\) matrix \(L\), the contraction. Its entry \(L_{ij} \in \{1, \dots, v\}\) is the row that holds check \(i\) in column \(j\). Expanding \(L\) places check \(i\) at field cell \((L_{ij}, j)\); the test entries fill the other \(T\) cells (Piepho and Williams 2026).

Reading the columns of \(L\) as blocks, \(L\) is a small block design for \(v\) “pseudo-treatments” (the field rows) in \(s\) blocks of size \(k\). For square fields this is the auxiliary block design of Bailey and Haines (2025).

FielDHub enforces a restricted placement. This is the restricted mode adopted for FielDHub, matching the binary contractions of Piepho and Williams (2026):

  • \(s \le v\);
  • no repeat within a column of \(L\): two checks never share a plot;
  • no repeat within a row of \(L\): no check appears twice in the same mathematical row;
  • balanced row loads: every \(r_h \ge 1\) and \(r_h \in \{\lfloor ks/v \rfloor, \lceil ks/v \rceil\}\), with \(\sum_h r_h = ks\). In words: every cross-line carries between \(\lfloor ks/v \rfloor\) and \(\lceil ks/v \rceil\) check plots, at least one.

Other placements, such as letting a check repeat within a cross-line, are not offered.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
\[y = X\tau + Z_R\rho + Z_C\gamma + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2 I),\]

with fixed treatment effects \(\tau\) (tests and checks), fixed row effects \(\rho\), fixed column effects \(\gamma\) and independent errors. \(X\) (\(n \times v^*\)), \(Z_R\) (\(n \times v\)) and \(Z_C\) (\(n \times s\)) are the plot-level design matrices.

The treatment information matrix is

\[C = \operatorname{diag}(u) - \frac{1}{s} M_R M_R^\mathsf{T} - \frac{1}{v} M_C M_C^\mathsf{T} + \frac{1}{n} u u^\mathsf{T}, \qquad M_R = X^\mathsf{T} Z_R, \quad M_C = X^\mathsf{T} Z_C.\]

All variances are reported in units of \(\sigma^2\): for treatments \(a\) and \(b\),

\[\operatorname{Var}(\hat\tau_a - \hat\tau_b)/\sigma^2 = (e_a - e_b)^\mathsf{T} C^{-} (e_a - e_b),\]

where \(e_a\) is the \(a\)-th unit vector and \(C^{-}\) a generalized inverse of \(C\).

docs.title: Connectivity and residual degrees of freedom
docs.text:
A design is connected when every treatment comparison is estimable. FielDHub decides this from the eigenvalues of an information matrix, not from a pivoted QR rank, and a design that is not connected is never scored or returned.

A connected design has

\[\mathrm{df} = ks - k - v - s + 2\]

residual degrees of freedom (the \(n\) plots minus the \(v^* + (v - 1) + (s - 1)\) estimated effects). It depends only on \(v\), \(s\) and \(k\), never on where the checks are placed.

Fields with \(\mathrm{df} < 1\) are rejected before any search: the residual variance could not be estimated. The section on residual degrees of freedom covers fields with fewer than 10.

docs.title: How FielDHub searches the check positions
docs.text:
The search works on the contraction \(L\), not on the full field. It keeps every candidate within the restricted placement rules and discards candidates that are not connected.

The available method is method = "staged": staged annealing with recoloring restarts. Each restart:

  • starts from a random balanced contraction;
  • anneals the column composition of \(L\) (which rows each column uses), scored by a fast column-design efficiency proxy;
  • re-arranges the rows of \(L\) by several random recolorings (re-assignments of which check takes which row within each column, keeping the column composition) and anneals the row arrangement under the chosen objective;
  • anneals rows and columns jointly under the chosen objective;
  • finishes with a short local polish that accepts only improvements.

In square fields (\(v = s\)) every row arrangement gives the same objective value, so the row phase is skipped and its share goes to the column phase.

Budget. budget is the number of objective-function calls allowed per location, shared by all restarts and phases; proxy calls count against it too. The search stops when the budget is spent. Final scoring of the returned design is outside the budget. The internal parameters (restarts, recolorings, phase shares, temperatures) are fixed by the package and are not user settings. When budget is not given, a default budget that depends on the field size is used; the rule is stated in ?augmented_row_column.

No silent fallback. If no connected starting design is found within a bounded number of tries, or the budget or time limit runs out before any design is produced, the function stops with a fieldhub_arc_search_error; it never switches to another method.

Only "staged" is accepted.

The search returns the best design it found within the budget; it does not prove that no better design exists.

docs.title: Randomization
docs.text:
After the search, from the same seed stream:

  • the mathematical rows and columns are permuted uniformly at random;
  • the \(k\) check labels receive one global random permutation;
  • the test entries are assigned to the test plots by a uniform random permutation;
  • the result is mapped to physical ROW and COLUMN.

Check occurrences are never shuffled one by one, because that could break the placement rules. None of these steps changes any objective value. Uniform row and column permutations give a valid randomization in the sense discussed by Bailey and Haines (2025) (their Section 3.3). The returned contraction and statistics describe the final, randomized placement, not the search’s internal output.

docs.title: Search objectives
docs.text:
The search optimizes one of three criteria, chosen with objective. All three, plus the check-versus-check variance and the two worst-case variances, are reported for every location whichever is optimized.

objective Definition Direction "V_tt" Mean of \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\tau_a - \hat\tau_b)/\sigma^2\) over all \(\binom{T}{2}\) pairs of test entries Minimize "V_tc" Mean over all \(Tk\) test-versus-check pairs Minimize "E_aug" Harmonic mean of the \(v^* - 1\) nonzero eigenvalues of \(A^* = \operatorname{diag}(u)^{-1/2}\, C \operatorname{diag}(u)^{-1/2}\): the average efficiency factor of Piepho and Williams (2026) Maximize

Reported only: V_cc (mean over the check pairs), max_tt and max_tc (largest test-versus-test and test-versus-check variance).

  • V_tt is the precision of comparisons among unreplicated entries, the usual purpose of a selection trial.
  • V_tc is the precision of comparing entries with the standard checks.
  • E_aug is the average efficiency relative to a completely randomized design with the same replications.

The criteria are related by

\[\frac{n(v^* - 1)}{E_{\mathrm{aug}}} = \sum_{i<j} u_i u_j \operatorname{Var}(\hat\tau_i - \hat\tau_j)/\sigma^2 .\]

E_aug therefore weights each test-versus-test pair by 1, each test-versus-check pair by \(s\) and each check-versus-check pair by \(s^2\), so it emphasizes comparisons involving checks more than V_tt does.

In square row- and column-binary designs the three criteria rank designs identically (Bailey and Haines 2025). In rectangular fields they can rank two designs differently, which is why all three are reported.

The default objective is currently "V_tt". Pass objective and budget explicitly when a result must be reproducible across package versions. Reproduction code always records both.

docs.title: Check direction
docs.text:
check_direction is required, with no default. It names the physical direction along which every check appears once per line:

  • "columns": each check appears once in every field column, so \(v\) = nrows and \(s\) = ncols;
  • "rows": each check appears once in every field row, so \(v\) = ncols and \(s\) = nrows.

The choice is never inferred from the field shape and the field is never turned silently. It is recorded in infoDesign, in the recorded parameters and in the CHECK_DIRECTION column of the field book.

The design needs \(s \le v\). A field and direction with \(s > v\) are rejected before any random number is drawn, with an error naming the other direction (see the examples below).

Choose the direction along which you want every check represented in every line, for example along the planting or harvesting pass.

ROW and COLUMN in the field book are always the physical field coordinates. Because the field book also carries CHECK_DIRECTION, a CSV export alone is enough to recompute the orientation and verify that each check appears once per line.

docs.title: Residual degrees of freedom
docs.text:
• \(\mathrm{df} < 1\): rejected (no residual variance estimate).
  • \(1 \le \mathrm{df} < 10\): allowed, with a warning (fieldhub_arc_low_df_warning) at construction, and a persistent notice printed by print() and summary() every time.

The warning states the df and, under independent normal errors, the relative standard deviation of the residual-variance estimate, \(\sqrt{2/\mathrm{df}}\) (about 82% at 3 df, 45% at 10 df).

Only adding a check or changing the number of rows or columns raises the residual degrees of freedom. Because df depends only on \(v\), \(s\) and \(k\), a longer search or another objective never changes it.

For example, the 12 × 8 field with three checks in the upload example below has \(\mathrm{df} = 3 \cdot 8 - 3 - 12 - 8 + 2 = 3\). This field geometry is one tabulated by Piepho and Williams (2026) (their Table 1).

docs.title: Use case
docs.text: A breeding program needs to test 80 lines with four checks at two locations, FARGO and CASSELTON, in a field of 12 rows and 10 columns at each location. Every check must appear once in every field column. The field has \(12 \times 10 = 120\) plots: each of the four checks takes one plot in each of the 10 columns (40 check plots), and the 80 lines fill the remaining plots. The design has \(4 \cdot 10 - 4 - 12 - 10 + 2 = 16\) residual degrees of freedom.

docs.title: Running the Shiny App
docs.text:
To launch the app you need to run either

FielDHub::run_app()

or

library(FielDHub)
run_app()

docs.title: 1. Using the FielDHub Shiny App
docs.text: Once the app is running, go to Unreplicated Designs > Augmented Row-Column.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
1. Import entries’ list? No generates labels from the counts. Yes uploads a .csv file with exactly the columns ENTRY and NAME (as for the diagonal arrangement): ENTRY distinct positive whole numbers, NAME distinct non-blank labels, the checks in the first rows. The file must have one row per check plus one row per test plot. This example shows the format with three checks and the first seven lines; a real file has one row per test plot.
ENTRY NAME 1 Check-1 2 Check-2 3 Check-3 4 Line 001 5 Line 002 6 Line 003 7 Line 004 8 Line 005 9 Line 006 10 Line 007
  1. Input # of Rows: and Input # of Columns: the field size (12 and 10 in the use case).
  2. Input # of Entries: the number of test entries (shown only without an upload). It must equal the number of test plots, \(T\) = rows × columns − checks × \(s\) (80).
  3. Input # of Checks: the number of checks, at least 2 (4).
  4. Each check appears once in every: column or row. No default: it must be chosen (column).
  5. Search objective: V_tt: test versus test variance, V_tc: test versus check variance or E_aug: efficiency of all comparisons. The value selected when the page opens is the default, V_tt.
  6. Input # of Locations: and the location names (2; FARGO, CASSELTON).
  7. Plot Order Layout: serpentine or cartesian.
  8. Starting Plot Number:, Input Experiment Name:, Random Seed: as in the other spatial designs (one starting plot per location, comma separated).
  9. Year (blank = current): the YEAR column; the effective year is recorded.
  10. Show advanced search options: reveals Search budget per location (blank = default): and Time limit per location in seconds (blank = none):. A blank budget uses the size-based default, and a time limit makes replay timing-dependent (see “Reproducing a design”).

Then, click Run!, then Randomize!. While the search runs the active tab shows “Searching for a balanced design…”; a field-scale search can take tens of seconds per location.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
After you run an augmented row-column design in FielDHub, the results are displayed in these tabs:

  • Get Random: the run controls and the design summary, which includes the per-location statistics and any low-df notice.
  • Data Input: the list of entries and the table of checks.
  • Field Layout: checks colored by check and tests in a neutral color, with PNG, PDF and CSV buttons at the top right.
  • Plot Number Field: the plot numbers laid out over the field.
  • Field Book: the full table, with the CHECK_DIRECTION column; downloadable as plain CSV.
  • Heatmap: simulated data, as on the other spatial pages.

The design can be downloaded as a saved result (RDS) or as a standalone R script; the section “Reproducing a design” explains what the script reproduces.

docs.title: 2. Using the FielDHub function: augmented_row_column()
docs.text:
First, load the package.

library(FielDHub)

docs.title: Inputs of augmented_row_column()
docs.text:
• checks: a count \(k \ge 2\) gives labels CH1, …, CHk; or a character vector of at least two distinct, non-missing, non-blank labels, used in that order.
  • entries: NULL (default) fills every test plot with labels G(k+1), …, G(k+T); a count must equal \(T\) and gives the same labels; a character vector of distinct labels must have length \(T\).
  • Check and test labels must differ. Labels are kept exactly as given, including spaces and punctuation, and are compared exactly.
  • data: an entry table with exactly the columns ENTRY | NAME. With data, checks must be the count \(k\) (the first \(k\) rows are the checks), and entries must be NULL; supplying both is an error naming the conflict, never a silent choice. The table must have \(k + T\) rows.
  • ENTRY in the field book: 1..k for checks and k+1..k+T for tests without data; the uploaded values with data.
  • exptName defaults to "Expt1", year to the current year, locationNames to 1..l; the effective values are recorded, so a later replay reproduces them.

Then, you can enter the information describing the above design like this. A small budget keeps this example fast; the objective and method are given explicitly so the example does not depend on the defaults.

arc <- augmented_row_column(
  nrows = 12,
  ncols = 10,
  checks = 4,
  check_direction = "columns",
  objective = "V_tt",
  method = "staged",
  budget = 500,
  l = 2,
  plotNumber = c(1001, 2001),
  locationNames = c("FARGO", "CASSELTON"),
  exptName = "ARC_2026",
  year = 2026,
  seed = 2026
)

docs.title: Details on the inputs entered in augmented_row_column() above
docs.text:
• nrows = 12, ncols = 10: the field size, 120 plots per location.
  • checks = 4: four checks, labeled CH1 to CH4.
  • check_direction = "columns": every check appears once in every field column, so \(v = 12\) and \(s = 10\).
  • entries is not given, so the 80 test plots get the labels G5 to G84.
  • objective = "V_tt": minimize the mean test-versus-test variance.
  • method = "staged": the only search method.
  • budget = 500: at most 500 objective calls per location. This is far below the default and is used only to keep the example fast; it says nothing about the quality of the result.
  • l = 2, plotNumber = c(1001, 2001), locationNames = c("FARGO", "CASSELTON"): two locations, each with its own first plot number.
  • exptName, year: recorded in the EXPT and YEAR columns.
  • seed = 2026: the seed. Location \(i\) runs with seed 2026 + i - 1.

docs.title: A direction that does not fit
docs.text:
Asking for each check once in every column of this 10 × 12 field needs at least 12 rows, so it is rejected before any search, and the message names the other direction:

augmented_row_column(
  nrows = 10,
  ncols = 12,
  checks = 4,
  check_direction = "columns",
  objective = "V_tt",
  method = "staged",
  budget = 500,
  seed = 7
)

Error in `arc_orient()`:
! With check_direction = "columns", every check appears once in each of the 12 field columns, which needs at least 12 field rows; the field has 10 (s = 12 > v = 10). Use check_direction = "rows", or change the numbers of rows and columns.

n_tests <- (12 - k) * 8
entries_list <- data.frame(
  ENTRY = seq_len(k + n_tests),
  NAME = c(paste0("Check-", seq_len(k)), sprintf("Line %03d", seq_len(n_tests)))
)

docs.title: Multiple locations
docs.text:
With l locations, the same search runs independently at each location with its own seed: the recorded seed plus the location index minus one (in the example, 2026 at FARGO and 2027 at CASSELTON).

Each location therefore has its own check positions, randomization, contraction, statistics, diagnostics and timing, all keyed by location name. The locations are not optimized jointly.

plotNumber takes one starting plot for all locations or one per location; locationNames one label per location.

budget and time_limit apply per location, so run time grows with l.

docs.title: Reproducing a design
docs.text:
Every result records its complete effective inputs in x$metadata$parameters, including the seed, objective, method, effective budget, check direction, effective year and location names. reproduce_design(x) and do.call(augmented_row_column, x$metadata$parameters) replay the design.

Exact replay. The replayed result is identical() (not equal within a tolerance) to the original in its deterministic content: everything except the timing element (wall-clock seconds) and the recorded package version. Deterministic content includes the field book, contraction, statistics, infoDesign, recorded parameters and RNG settings, and the diagnostics counters and statuses.

When it holds. For runs stopped by the evaluation budget, in which no location reached time_limit, and within the same software and numerical environment: the same FielDHub version, R version, BLAS/LAPACK library and thread count, and platform.

A time_limit cutoff makes replay timing-dependent: how far the search got depends on the machine and its load. time_limit bounds each location’s search only (final scoring, randomization and field-book assembly always complete), so a call with l locations can take about l * time_limit seconds plus that work.

Across environments there is no promise of the same design. Small numerical differences can change search decisions, not only final scores. Replay in another environment gives a valid design with comparable statistics, which may be a different design. This is also why the numbers printed in this vignette can differ from those on another computer.

replay <- reproduce_design(arc_rows)
identical(replay$fieldBook, arc_rows$fieldBook)

[1] TRUE

identical(replay$contraction, arc_rows$contraction)

[1] TRUE

identical(replay$statistics, arc_rows$statistics)

[1] TRUE

identical(replay$diagnostics, arc_rows$diagnostics)

[1] TRUE

identical(replay$metadata$parameters, arc_rows$metadata$parameters)

[1] TRUE

names(arc_rows$timing)

[1] "LOCATION"     "search"       "verification" "total"

timing holds the search, verification and total seconds of each location. It is kept apart from the rest of the result precisely so that the deterministic content can be compared exactly.

docs.title: Standalone reproduction code
docs.text:
write_design(x, file, format = "r") writes a standalone R script that rebuilds the design from the recorded parameters; the app’s R-script download produces the same script.

Standalone code is available for the standard entry template at any size, and for any upload up to 200 rows.

  • An upload whose ENTRY values are exactly 1, ..., k + T in row order is recorded as its check and test labels with data = NULL, so its script is standalone at any field size, and replay from the labels gives identical deterministic content.
  • An upload with other ENTRY values is recorded as uploaded. Up to 200 rows its script is standalone; above 200 rows no standalone script is produced, and the saved result (RDS, write_design(x, file)) is the way to keep the design. The app states this reason in place of the script.

The RDS file preserves the result itself and does not depend on replay.

script <- tempfile(fileext = ".R")
write_design(arc_rows, script, format = "r")
cat(readLines(script), sep = "\n")

# FielDHub version: 1.7.5
# Replays recorded inputs; numerical results can depend on software versions.
design <- local({
  .rng_kind <- RNGkind()
  .had_seed <- exists(".Random.seed", globalenv(), inherits = FALSE)
  .rng_seed <- if (.had_seed) get(".Random.seed", globalenv())
  on.exit({
    do.call(RNGkind, as.list(.rng_kind))
    if (.had_seed) assign(".Random.seed", .rng_seed, globalenv())
    else if (exists(".Random.seed", globalenv(), inherits = FALSE))
      rm(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())
  }, add = TRUE)
  .recorded_kind <- as.list(unname(c("Mersenne-Twister", "Inversion", "Rejection")))
  if (length(.recorded_kind) == 4L && !"binom.kind" %in% names(formals(RNGkind)))
    stop("The recorded binomial RNG requires R >= 4.7.")
  if (length(.recorded_kind) == 3L && "binom.kind" %in% names(formals(RNGkind)))
    .recorded_kind[[4L]] <- "Buggy BTPE"
  do.call(RNGkind, .recorded_kind)
  FielDHub::augmented_row_column(
    nrows = 10,
    ncols = 12,
    checks = c("Check A", "Check B", "Check C", "Check D"),
    check_direction = "rows",
    objective = "E_aug",
    budget = 500,
    locationNames = 1L,
    exptName = "Expt1",
    year = "2026",
    seed = 7
  )
})

unlink(script)
